title: UAE Retail T-Sukuk at 5.06%: what individual investors should know
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: The UAE's second sovereign retail sukuk offers a fixed 5.06% a year over five years from AED 1,000. How it works, what the first issuance showed, and the trade-offs to weigh before subscriptions close on 28 September.
body_html:
5.06%Annual profit rate, fixed
5 yearsTenor to maturity
AED 1,000Minimum subscription
23–28 SepSubscription window, 2026
Twice a yearProfit distributions
1 OctListing on Nasdaq Dubai

For most of the UAE's history, government debt has been an institutional market. Banks, pension funds and asset managers bought sovereign paper; individual savers did not. The Ministry of Finance's Sovereign Retail T-Sukuk Programme changes that, putting AED-denominated, government-backed Islamic securities within reach of anyone with AED 1,000 and a UAE investor account.

The second issuance, priced on 22 September, targets AED 50 million and pays a fixed 5.06% a year over five years, distributed every six months. It is open to UAE nationals and residents.

The two issuances side by side

First issuanceSecond issuance
Subscription window24–30 June 202623–28 September 2026
Annual profit rate4.30%5.06%
Tenor2 years5 years
Target sizeAED 50M (raised to AED 100M)AED 50M
MinimumAED 1,000AED 1,000
PayoutsSemi-annualSemi-annual
ListingNasdaq Dubai, 2 July 2026Nasdaq Dubai, 1 October 2026

The higher rate is not a sweetener. It is largely the price of time: investors committing capital for five years rather than two are paid a term premium, and the Ministry says the rate was set in line with prevailing market conditions.

What the first issuance told us

The June offering was the proof of concept, and demand was emphatic. Orders reached AED 445 million against a AED 50 million target, close to nine times oversubscribed, and the Ministry doubled the issue to AED 100 million.

The subscriber mix matters as much as the headline number. Investors placing AED 10,000 or less made up 76% of all subscribers, UAE nationals accounted for 72%, and investors under 25 together with women made up 45%. This was genuinely retail money, which is the point of the programme: building a domestic savings culture and a deeper AED capital market.

What the numbers look like

Because the rate is fixed and paid semi-annually, the cash flow is easy to model. Figures below are gross, assume the full amount is allocated and the sukuk is held to maturity, and do not reinvest payouts.

InvestedEvery six monthsPer yearOver five years
AED 1,000AED 25.30AED 50.60AED 253

Why it appeals

Sovereign credit

The instrument is backed by the UAE Government, which places its credit risk at the lowest end of anything available to a UAE retail investor.

A low entry point

AED 1,000 is a fraction of what most fixed-income products demand for comparable yields, which is why small tickets dominated the first issuance.

Shariah compliance

Returns are structured as profit rather than interest, giving investors who avoid conventional bonds a clean sovereign option.

Predictable income

A fixed rate paid twice a year is simple to plan around, whether for household budgeting or a longer-term savings ladder.

The trade-offs

Low credit risk is not the same as no risk. Four things deserve attention before subscribing.

Selling early can mean a loss

Face value is repaid at maturity. Before then, the price on Nasdaq Dubai moves with interest rates. If rates rise over the next five years, a 5.06% sukuk becomes less attractive and may trade below what you paid. The protection only works if you can hold for the full term.

Liquidity can be thin

Market makers and liquidity providers support trading, but retail sukuk markets are young. Finding a buyer at a fair price mid-term may be slower or costlier than expected.

You may not get your full allocation

If this issuance is oversubscribed like the first, applications may be scaled back. Allocation is set for 29 September, with excess funds refunded on 30 September, so the uninvested remainder comes back as cash.

Inflation is the quiet risk

A fixed 5.06% protects you if deposit rates fall, but leaves you exposed if inflation runs above that level. Over five years, that is real purchasing power.

The operator's view. Treat this as the anchor of a savings plan, not the whole plan. It suits money you are confident you will not need for five years. For funds you may need sooner, the shorter first issuance on the secondary market or a laddered approach across future issuances may fit better.

How to subscribe

Subscriptions run until 28 September 2026 through the DFM eIPO platform, the iVestor app, the DFM app, and the digital channels of the receiving banks. Emirates NBD is lead receiving bank, with Emirates Islamic, Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank, Ajman Bank, Mashreq, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank and First Abu Dhabi Bank participating. Units are credited to investor accounts after allocation and before listing.

This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial, investment or Shariah advice. OM4Biz is not a licensed financial adviser. Figures are drawn from public Ministry of Finance announcements as of 24 September 2026; confirm terms with the issuer or your bank before investing.

title: The Real Cost of Growing Old in the UAE: What Long-Term Expats Are Up Against
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: UAE retiree health cover averages USD 9,470 a year — among the priciest in the world — and long-term expats have no state pension, no portable social security, and residency tied to a financial threshold. What the numbers show, and how to plan around the gap.
body_html:
USD 9,470Avg. annual retiree health cover, UAE
Dh45,000Typical 65+ comprehensive plan/year
Dh1MProperty/savings threshold, retirement visa
Dh20,000Alternative monthly income threshold
0%Tax on pensions, dividends, investment returns
0UAE social security totalisation agreements with major sending countries

The UAE was built as a place people come to work, not a place they grow old. For decades that was the whole arrangement: earn, save, remit, and eventually leave. A growing share of its residents no longer fit that script. They arrived in their twenties, raised families here, built businesses here, and are now approaching retirement age with no state pension, no UAE social security record that travels home, and a healthcare bill that rises sharply with every year past sixty. The gap between what long-term expats have built here and what the system offers them in old age is widening, and it is worth understanding in detail — both as a personal planning problem and as an operating one for any UAE business with a tenured expat workforce.

How UAE retirement costs compare globally

Health insurance is the single biggest recurring cost of growing old in the UAE, and it is not close to the cheapest option available to a globally mobile retiree. A Pacific Prime study ranks the UAE the 14th most expensive country worldwide for international health insurance for retirees, at an average USD 9,470 a year. That is less than half the US figure (USD 23,231), but several multiples of the cost in the retirement destinations expats most often compare it to.

MarketTypical retiree health coverAnnualised (approx.)
United States—USD 23,231 / yr
UAE (average, all ages)—USD 9,470 / yr
UAE (comprehensive plan, 65+)—~ USD 12,250 / yr (Dh45,000)
Spain / Portugal~ €559 / mo~ USD 7,200 / yr
Mexico / Costa Rica~ €335 / mo~ USD 4,300 / yr

The spread matters more at 65+, where UAE premiums climb fastest. A comprehensive plan for a retiree in that bracket can reach Dh45,000 (about USD 12,250) a year — roughly the entire annual cost of comparable cover in Mexico or Costa Rica, doubled.

The trade-off: lifestyle against financial security

Almost no long-term expat frames the decision to stay as purely financial. It rarely is.

Why people stay

For residents who have spent twenty or thirty years here, the UAE is simply home — children were raised, careers were built, and the emotional ties run deeper than a posting. It is also a genuinely favourable place to hold wealth: there is no income tax on pensions, dividends or investment returns, which stretches whatever retirement savings a resident has accumulated. And the practical case is real too — world-class private healthcare infrastructure, a large English-speaking community, and among the highest personal safety standards anywhere.

What staying actually costs

Three structural gaps sit underneath the lifestyle case. First, there is no state pension: end-of-service gratuity, personal savings and whatever international pension a resident has kept up are the entire retirement system. Second, healthcare cost rises exactly when income typically falls, and for retirees on a fixed income it can become the deciding factor in whether to stay. Third, residency itself is conditional rather than guaranteed — it depends on clearing a financial threshold (Dh1 million in property or savings, or Dh20,000 in monthly income for the retirement visa route) and maintaining continuous health insurance without a lapse, which itself can jeopardise the visa.

The structural policy gap

The underlying issue is a mismatch of design and reality. UAE residency policy was built around temporary labour migration — workers arriving for a contract, then leaving. A large and growing share of the expat population no longer moves through the system that way; they are multi-generational, long-tenure residents whose working lives were spent entirely inside the UAE economy.

That population has no clean path to old-age protection. There is no mechanism to aggregate years of UAE residency with home-country pension contributions, because the UAE has no social security totalisation agreements with the countries that send it the most long-term residents, India among them. For many lower- and middle-income long-tenure workers, the honest retirement plan is simply to keep working as long as possible — not for income alone, but because employment is what keeps the visa, and the visa is what keeps the healthcare access, active.

The practical effect is a transfer of responsibility. Decades of economic contribution happen inside the UAE; the cost of old age, when it arrives, is quietly pushed back onto the home country or onto whatever the individual managed to save privately.

A practical path forward

Plan from year one, not year fifty-five

Retirement planning has to be treated as a personal responsibility from the first UAE payslip, not something addressed once retirement is a few years away. The tax-free structure rewards early, disciplined saving far more than it rewards catching up late.

Build savings that don't depend on residency

International pension schemes and investments held outside the UAE system protect income regardless of where a resident eventually retires — UAE, home country, or a third location. Portability is the entire point; a plan that only works if the visa holds is not a plan.

Budget for healthcare as a core line item, not a surprise

Health insurance cost in the UAE does not rise gently with age — it climbs sharply after sixty. Modelling that increase into a retirement budget in advance, rather than discovering it at renewal time, is the difference between a manageable plan and a forced decision to leave.

The operator's view. This is not only a personal-finance story — it is a workforce-retention one. Any UAE employer with long-tenured expat staff is, in effect, competing against this exact gap every time a senior employee starts doing the arithmetic on staying past fifty. Structuring end-of-service benefits, voluntary savings plans and senior-tier health cover deliberately — rather than leaving them at statutory minimums — is one of the more underused levers UAE employers have for retaining the institutional knowledge that a decade-plus employee actually represents.
